paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of charge
paragraphs.text: Electric charge is a property of matter that makes it feel a force when it sits in an electromagnetic field. It comes in two kinds, positive and negative. Charges of the same kind push each other away, and opposite charges pull together. An object with no overall charge is called electrically neutral.

paragraphs.heading: Who carries it
paragraphs.text: In ordinary matter, electrons carry negative charge and protons, in the nuclei of atoms, carry positive charge. A piece of matter with more electrons than protons is negative, one with fewer is positive, and one with equal numbers is neutral. The charge of a large object is just the sum of the charges of its particles. That total is often small, because atoms usually hold equal numbers of protons and electrons, so their charges cancel.

paragraphs.heading: Charge comes in steps
paragraphs.text: Charge is quantized: it comes only in whole-number multiples of a tiny unit, the elementary charge e. One e is about 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C. The proton carries +e and the electron carries −e. Quarks have smaller charges, in steps of 1/3 e, but they are only found joined into particles whose total charge is a whole multiple of e. Michael Faraday was the first to notice that charge comes in separate pieces, in his electrolysis experiments. Robert Millikan's oil drop experiment later showed it directly and measured e.

paragraphs.heading: It never disappears
paragraphs.text: In an isolated system, the total charge stays fixed. Subtract all the negative charge from all the positive charge, and the answer never changes over time. The Standard Model treats charge as a quantum number that is conserved absolutely.

paragraphs.heading: Ions
paragraphs.text: When an atom, or a cluster of atoms, loses electrons, it ends up positive and is called a cation. One that has gained electrons ends up negative, and is called an anion. Both are ions. Ions made from a single atom are monatomic, while those made from two or more bonded atoms are polyatomic.

paragraphs.heading: Static electricity
paragraphs.text: When an object carries a net charge that is not moving, we call it static electricity. Rubbing two different materials together, like amber with fur or glass with silk, makes it easily. Charge moves from one material to the other and leaves behind an equal and opposite charge. Before electrons and protons were discovered, Benjamin Franklin defined positive charge as the charge a glass rod picks up when rubbed with silk.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring charge
paragraphs.text: The SI unit of charge is the coulomb, C, named after the French physicist Charles-Augustin de Coulomb. Electrical engineers often use the ampere-hour instead. Physicists and chemists also count charge in elementary charges. Chemists use the Faraday constant too, equal to the charge carried by a mole of elementary charges.
